### Live Synthesis: Transmission Congestion & Market Dynamics

Northern nodes are demonstrating robust clean generation, with Scottish wind output surging to 4,350.8 MW and depressing regional carbon intensity to an optimal 32 gCO2/kWh. While this highlights Scotland’s essential contribution to national decarbonisation, the high volume exacerbates acute structural imbalances across the wider GB transmission network.

Export capability across the Cheviot boundary (B6) remains saturated. Physical thermal limitations prevent this northern surplus from evacuating south toward high-demand load centres in England. Consequently, the National Energy System Operator (NESO) is forced to resolve the bottleneck via the Balancing Mechanism—paying northern wind assets to curtail generation while simultaneously compensating thermal plants south of the constraint to ramp up.

This structural friction has driven instantaneous constraint costs to £29,848.5. These operational interventions are not absorbed by generators; they are recovered through Balancing Services Use of System (BSUoS) charges and ultimately passed directly onto consumer electricity bills. Until planned grid reinforcement projects—notably the Eastern Green Link HVDC conduits—come online, periods of peak northern wind will continue to expose this costly friction between renewable generation capacity and physical transmission infrastructure.
